question: The Commission is promoting the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in defence, in particular under the European Defence Fund and in the ‘White Paper for European Defence – Readiness 2030’. At the same time, military applications are expressly excluded from the scope of the AI Act.

Indeed, Article 7 of the act requires that supported measures be compatible with international law and ethical principles, while Article 10 contains no specific provisions on AI or autonomous weapon systems. Meanwhile, Parliament expressly called for a ban on lethal autonomous weapon systems in its resolution of 20 January 2021 and stressed the need for rigorous human oversight. 1.

How does Commission explain the fact that military applications are excluded from the scope of the AI Act at the same time as AI-based defence technologies are being supported by the European Defence Fund?
How are Parliament’s calls for restrictions or even a ban on autonomous weapon systems being taken into account in AI advancements in defence?

What requirements are in place for EU-funded defence projects to ensure clear responsibilities, sufficient human oversight, and transparency over the allocation of EU funds, and is the Commission planning further legislation or will the existing regulatory gaps remain?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.

2026) Recital 24 of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act (2024/1689)1 clarifies why military and defence applications are not included in the Act: ‘As regards military and defence purposes, such exclusion is justified both by Article 4(2) of the Treaty on the European Union (TEU)2 and by the specificities of the Member States’ and the common Union defence policy covered by Chapter 2 of Title V TEU that are subject to public international law, which is therefore the more appropriate legal framework for the regulation of AI systems in the context of the use of lethal force and other AI systems in the context of military and defence activities’.

The European defence industrial programmes do not fund actions related to defence products that are prohibited by applicable international law. These programmes, moreover, lay down specific provisions regarding lethal autonomous weapons.

The European Defence Fund specifically bans the EU funding of lethal autonomous weapons without the possibility of human control over the selection and engagement decisions when carrying out strikes against humans. Furthermore, as part of an ethics review, the Commission screens all proposals, with support of external ethics experts, to identify those actions raising complex or serious ethical issues.

Actions which are not ethically acceptable will be rejected. In addition, the European Defence Industry Programme3 cannot fund defence products which are prohibited by applicable international law, nor lethal autonomous systems that operate outside a responsible chain of human command and control or cannot comply with the principles of International Humanitarian Law.
